c0014: Growth in events in year 3 over year 2, kept conservative for the same reason: repeat corporate clients and planner referrals build up slowly.
c0032: Card and ACH fees on total sales. Many companies pay by ACH or check, which lowers the cost; cards cost more. The example (2.5%) is a blended rate: a percentage plus a per-transaction fee, which weighs more on small invoices. Check your processor's statement and enter your effective rate (Kit estimate).
c0053: Your own money. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection (often around 10% for SBA start-ups; many want 20-30%) on the total cash needed in this plan.
c0061: ZERO by default: repayment starts in year 1, so the year-1 DSCR already measures the full loan payment. If you negotiate an interest-only first year, enter it here and read the year-1 DSCR with care.
c0063: The minimum this workbook asks for (see "Instructions"): a cushion below 3 months does not cover a slow stretch, such as the off-season for weddings or a corporate client who pays late.
c0108: Only used if you enter alcohol sales above, which is zero in this plan. Example rate: the same as the rest of the sales (state + local combined). Some states tax alcohol at a different rate or add liquor taxes: if you sell alcohol, enter the rate that applies.
c0117: Enter the minimum wage of your state or city, annualized for a full-time job (hourly rate × 2,080 hours). The pay floor in the "Staffing" tab is the HIGHER of this cell and the federal minimum. With 0 or blank, the traffic light compares only against the federal floor. Check current rates at dol.gov.
c0124: Enter a whole number from 1 to 365: guests per event or days.
c0157: State filing fees for the articles of organization (Secretary of State) plus any attorney or filing-service fees; a registered agent is also needed. Fees vary a lot by state. The "Taxable / recoverable tax?" column is set to No: it only matters if you enter a recoverable input tax rate (for example UK VAT).
c0309: Events per year needed to cover costs for each price per guest (columns, in steps around the plan's price) and each variable cost per guest (rows). Green cells are below the events per year the plan forecasts.
c0310: Events per year needed: price per guest excl. sales tax (columns) × variable cost per guest (rows)
c0326: Guests each full-time equivalent in the "Staffing" table would have to serve in a year. In the optimistic scenario it tells you whether you need to hire
c0331: The "Base" column reads its three inputs (events per year, price per guest and guests per event) from the "0. Assumptions" tab, so it reproduces EXACTLY year 1 of the P&L. The other two scenarios use the same cost rates: only events, price and guests change. FIXED COSTS are the same in all three, while variable costs follow the sales of each scenario.
c0360: 40 hours a week is the FLSA overtime threshold for non-exempt employees; some states add daily overtime rules. Change it if your own full-time week is different
c0364: Hours of work that one event needs: shopping, prep, loading, transport, setup, service, breakdown and cleanup. Serving is only part of it. Hours × people × events per year sets the event staff cost.
c0366: Average number of people working each event. A large wedding needs more hands: raise it here and the staffing sizes itself.
c0381: 3. Only "Break-Even" is derived entirely from the rest. The other three tabs also have green cells you can edit: the pessimistic and optimistic scenarios in "Scenarios", seasonality and the launch ramp-up in "12-Month Cash Flow", and the other funding sources in "Financing" (rows 8-11 count as sources but are not amortized: your bank or SBA 7(a) loan goes in "Loan requested" on "0. Assumptions"). Everything else is calculated.
c0386: 8. The Word business plan in this kit uses the same example figures as this workbook. The workbook is the one that recalculates on its own when you change a green cell: if you change one, update the matching figures in the Word document.
c0397: Events per year for the ACCOUNTING break-even (depreciation included)
c0404: A typed-in number that does not match the Staffing tab
c0405: Read directly from the Staffing tab
c0406: If you change a salary, the whole plan recalculates, so the P&L and the staffing table can never disagree.
c0408: One line called "staff", with no link to event hours or pay floors
c0409: Positions with their FTE, sized to the hours your events need, with event staff paid per event
c0410: A plan staffed for fewer hours than it sells does not work on its own numbers. This layout makes that gap visible before a lender does.
c0412: Sales typed as one lump sum, with no link to bookings
c0413: Revenue = events per year × guests per event × price per guest, one cell each for the whole workbook
c0414: Break-even, scenarios and the P&L read the same three cells, so they always agree, and you can see which lever moves the result: more events, bigger events or a higher price.
c0416: A price with no statement of whether sales tax or service is included
c0417: Declared EXCL. sales tax, with service included and the voluntary gratuity left out
c0418: Declaring it changes no number: it just says what the number is. Price per guest incl. sales tax = price per guest × (1 + sales tax rate), and the workbook calculates it for you.
c0420: Left out: the model shows no cost of space
c0424: A round number labeled "3 months" that does not match the fixed costs
c0425: Three months of cash fixed costs, calculated by formula
c0426: A round number often covers far less than the label says. This cushion is what keeps you open through a slow month between wedding seasons.
c0428: One useful life for everything, including items that are not fixed assets
c0432: Counted twice: once in startup costs and again as an annual expense
c0433: Counted once, as an annual expense
c0434: Counting a premium in both places inflates the startup costs, the cash you need to raise and the loan you ask for.
c0436: A separate line, on top of utilities
c0438: Writing it in two places counts it twice: here it lives in one cell and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0440: A lump sum typed by hand
c0444: A flat rate every year, with no offset for losses
c0445: One effective rate for years 1-2 and another from year 3, offsetting net operating losses carried forward
c0446: A loss in one year reduces taxable profit in later years. The model offsets losses fully as a simplification (federal rules cap the offset at 80% of taxable income). If you operate as a pass-through (sole proprietorship or LLC), set the rate to 0 and budget your personal tax separately.
c0448: The full payment deducted in the P&L
c0449: Only interest in the P&L; principal repaid in the cash flow
c0450: Putting the full payment above the line turns the P&L into a cash flow, and a lender spots it immediately.
c0453: A dedicated tab: where the money comes from, what it pays for and the amortization schedule year by year
c0454: It is the sheet a lender asks for next to the P&L, and it warns you when the money you put in falls short of what you need.
c0457: A 12-month tab: cash in, cash out, quarterly sales tax and the cumulative balance
c0458: It answers the one question that decides a loan: in which month does the business run out of cash?
c0460: Fuel and a miscellaneous line typed in among the fixed costs
c0461: One percentage of sales, treated as a variable cost
c0463: Cost of goods on all sales
c0464: Revenue with no cost of goods sold attached
c0466: A revenue line that pays for no ingredients shows a margin that does not exist.
c0468: Wages never compared with any legal floor
c0469: No row below the pay floor in proportion to its FTE, and a cell for your state or local minimum wage
c0470: State and local minimums are often higher than the federal one: enter yours in "0. Assumptions" and the traffic light warns you when a wage falls short.
